claim: There are approximately 4.95 million fatalities associated with antibiotic-resistant bacteria worldwide each year.
source: There are approximately 4.95 million fatalities associated with antibiotic-resistant bacteria worldwide each year (Murray et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Murray et al., 2022.

claim: The high mortality rate from antibiotic-resistant bacteria contrasts with the low development rate of new antibacterial agents for clinical applications.
source: This high mortality rate contrasts with the low development rate of new antibacterial agents for clinical applications (WHO, 2022; Beyer and Paulin, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to WHO, 2022 and Beyer and Paulin, 2020.

claim: Mining natural microbial communities has become a promising endeavor in the hunt for novel antimicrobials.
source: Mining natural microbial communities has become a promising endeavor in the hunt for novel antimicrobials because most microbes deploy bioactive compounds to contend with their competitors in the diverse assemblies they live in.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about microbial competition and secondary metabolites.

claim: Most microbes deploy bioactive compounds to contend with their competitors in the diverse assemblies they live in.
source: Mining natural microbial communities has become a promising endeavor in the hunt for novel antimicrobials because most microbes deploy bioactive compounds to contend with their competitors in the diverse assemblies they live in.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about microbial ecology.

claim: Competition for iron is a main determinant of species interactions in soil and freshwater communities.
source: For example, there is increasing evidence that competition for iron is a main determinant of species interactions in soil and freshwater communities (Butaitė et al., 2017; Deveau et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Butaitė et al., 2017 and Deveau et al., 2016.

claim: Siderophores are a class of secondary metabolites that scavenges environmental iron with high affinity.
source: Competition for iron involves the secretion of siderophores, a class of secondary metabolites that scavenges environmental iron with high affinity (Hider and Kong, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hider and Kong, 2010.

claim: Siderophores are often species specific.
source: Because siderophores are often species specific, they have two opposing effects: they make iron available for related community members possessing the matching receptor but withhold iron from competitors with non-matching receptors.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about siderophore specificity.

claim: Siderophores make iron available for related community members possessing the matching receptor but withhold iron from competitors with non-matching receptors.
source: Because siderophores are often species specific, they have two opposing effects: they make iron available for related community members possessing the matching receptor but withhold iron from competitors with non-matching receptors.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the species-specific nature of siderophores.

claim: Siderophores can be competitive agents in inter-species interactions.
source: Thus, siderophores can be competitive agents in inter-species interactions (Figueiredo et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2012; Niehus et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Figueiredo et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2012; Niehus et al., 2017.

claim: Pyoverdines are a class of siderophores with high iron affinity that are produced and secreted by fluorescent Pseudomonas spp. under iron-limited conditions.
source: Specifically, we investigate whether siderophores from non-pathogenic environmental bacteria can induce iron starvation and growth arrest in human pathogens. We focus on pyoverdines, a class of siderophores with high iron affinity that are produced and secreted by fluorescent Pseudomonas spp. under iron-limited conditions (Visca et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Visca et al., 2007.

claim: Upon complexation with ferric iron, the iron-loaded pyoverdine is imported into the cell by receptors with high specificity and subsequently reduced to the bio-available ferrous iron.
source: Upon complexation with ferric iron, the iron-loaded pyoverdine is imported into the cell by receptors with high specificity and subsequently reduced to the bio-available ferrous iron (Bonneau et al., 2020; Cornelis et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bonneau et al., 2020 and Cornelis et al., 2023.

claim: Pyoverdines show an extraordinary structural diversity with more than 70 described variants that differ in their peptide backbone.
source: Pyoverdines show an extraordinary structural diversity with more than 70 described variants that differ in their peptide backbone (Meyer et al., 2008; Rehm et al., 2022) and have an extremely high affinity for iron (Ka = 1032 M–1, pyoverdine produced by Pseudomonas fluorescens biotype B) (Meyer and Abdallah, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meyer et al., 2008 and Rehm et al., 2022.

claim: Pyoverdines have an extremely high affinity for iron (Ka = 1032 M–1, pyoverdine produced by Pseudomonas fluorescens biotype B).
source: Pyoverdines show an extraordinary structural diversity with more than 70 described variants that differ in their peptide backbone (Meyer et al., 2008; Rehm et al., 2022) and have an extremely high affinity for iron (Ka = 1032 M–1, pyoverdine produced by Pseudomonas fluorescens biotype B) (Meyer and Abdallah, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meyer and Abdallah, 1978.

claim: A screen of 320 natural Pseudomonas isolates used against 12 human pathogens uncovered several pyoverdines with particularly high antibacterial properties and distinct chemical characteristics.
source: A screen of 320 natural Pseudomonas isolates used against 12 human pathogens uncovered several pyoverdines with particularly high antibacterial properties and distinct chemical characteristics.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the screening assay described in the manuscript.

claim: The most potent pyoverdine effectively reduced growth of the pathogens Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus in a concentration- and iron-dependent manner.
source: The most potent pyoverdine effectively reduced growth of the pathogens Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus in a concentration- and iron-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dose-response experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Pyoverdine increased survival of infected Galleria mellonella host larvae.
source: Pyoverdine increased survival of infected Galleria mellonella host larvae and showed low toxicity for the host, mammalian cell lines, and erythrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from infection experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Pyoverdine showed low toxicity for the host, mammalian cell lines, and erythrocytes.
source: Pyoverdine increased survival of infected Galleria mellonella host larvae and showed low toxicity for the host, mammalian cell lines, and erythrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from toxicity assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Experimental evolution of pathogens combined with whole-genome sequencing revealed limited resistance evolution compared to an antibiotic.
source: Furthermore, experimental evolution of pathogens combined with whole-genome sequencing revealed limited resistance evolution compared to an antibiotic.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from experimental evolution experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pyoverdines from environmental strains have the potential to become a new class of sustainable antibacterials against specific human pathogens.
source: Thus, pyoverdines from environmental strains have the potential to become a new class of sustainable antibacterials against specific human pathogens.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The 320 Pseudomonas isolates stem from freshwater and soil communities and belong to the group of fluorescent pseudomonads.
source: The isolates stem from freshwater and soil communities and belong to the group of fluorescent pseudomonads (e.g., P. fluorescens, P. putida, P. syringae, P. chlororaphis) that are non-pathogenic to humans and can produce and secrete pyoverdines, a group of high iron-affinity siderophores (Meyer, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meyer, 2000 and previous characterization work.

claim: Fluorescent pseudomonads are non-pathogenic to humans and can produce and secrete pyoverdines.
source: The isolates stem from freshwater and soil communities and belong to the group of fluorescent pseudomonads (e.g., P. fluorescens, P. putida, P. syringae, P. chlororaphis) that are non-pathogenic to humans and can produce and secrete pyoverdines, a group of high iron-affinity siderophores (Meyer, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meyer, 2000.

claim: Several isolates are likely to produce secondary siderophores in addition to pyoverdine.
source: Important to note is that several isolates are likely to produce secondary siderophores in addition to pyoverdine (Cornelis, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cornelis, 2010.

claim: Secondary siderophores generally have lower iron affinity than pyoverdine.
source: Given that secondary siderophores generally have lower iron affinity than pyoverdine, we anticipate treatment effects to be primarily driven by pyoverdines.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about siderophore iron affinities.

claim: Treatment effects are anticipated to be primarily driven by pyoverdines rather than secondary siderophores.
source: Given that secondary siderophores generally have lower iron affinity than pyoverdine, we anticipate treatment effects to be primarily driven by pyoverdines.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the relative iron affinities of pyoverdines and secondary siderophores.

claim: High variation in the supernatant effect was found, ranging from complete pathogen growth inhibition to growth promotion compared to the control treatment.
source: We found high variation in the supernatant effect, ranging from complete pathogen growth inhibition to growth promotion compared to the control treatment (70% CAA supplemented with 30% sodium chloride 0.8% solution) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mean supernatant effect across all pathogens showed a bimodal distribution with two peaks at 0.47–0.58 (approximately 50% growth inhibition) and 1.00–1.10 (no growth inhibition).
source: The mean supernatant effect across all pathogens showed a bimodal distribution with two peaks at 0.47–0.58 (approximately 50% growth inhibition) and 1.00–1.10 (no growth inhibition) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Supernatants containing siderophores can have both growth inhibitory and stimulatory effects.
source: Our observations are consistent with previous studies, in which supernatants containing siderophores can have both growth inhibitory and stimulatory effects (Gu et al., 2020; Butaitė et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gu et al., 2020 and Butaitė et al., 2018.

claim: 25 supernatants inhibited all 12 pathogens.
source: For each supernatant, we quantified the number of pathogens that experienced a growth reduction of at least 20% compared to the control and found that 25 supernatants inhibited all 12 pathogens (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Seven top candidate supernatants were identified for which a relative growth recovery of at least 0.2 occurred for all 12 pathogens under iron-replete conditions.
source: We identified seven top candidate supernatants for which a relative growth recovery of at least 0.2 occurred for all 12 pathogens (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Growth recovery in iron-rich medium indicates that pyoverdines are involved in growth inhibition in iron-limited medium.
source: Growth recovery in iron-rich medium indicates that pyoverdines are involved in growth inhibition in iron-limited medium.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the experimental design and results.

claim: Among the remaining 18 supernatants, the overall rate of growth recovery was also high, indicating that pyoverdines are responsible for pathogen growth inhibition under iron-limited conditions in most cases.
source: Among the remaining 18 supernatants, the overall rate of growth recovery was also high, indicating that pyoverdines are responsible for pathogen growth inhibition under iron-limited conditions in most cases.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Growth inhibitory effects were not restricted to a few closely related strains but were scattered across the phylogenetic tree.
source: We found that growth inhibitory effects were not restricted to a few closely related strains but were scattered across the phylogenetic tree.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a certain level of clustering with two Pseudomonas spp. clades showing an accumulation of strains with growth-inhibitory effects on pathogens.
source: Nonetheless, there was a certain level of clustering with two Pseudomonas spp. clades showing an accumulation of strains with growth-inhibitory effects on pathogens.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Closely as well as distantly related strains can produce inhibitory pyoverdines.
source: This analysis suggests that closely as well as distantly related strains can produce inhibitory pyoverdines.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The seven top candidate supernatants yielded five structurally different pyoverdines.
source: These studies included the pyoverdines extracted from the seven top candidate supernatants and the analysis therein yielded five structurally different pyoverdines (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical structure elucidation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: One novel pyoverdine type (1, from isolate 3A06) was found.
source: We found one novel pyoverdine type (1, from isolate 3A06) and four pyoverdine types already known from the literature (2–5).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical structure elucidation data.

claim: The pyoverdine from isolate 3G07 can occur in either a linear or cyclic conformation (2a and 2b).
source: The pyoverdine from isolate 3G07 can occur in either a linear or cyclic conformation (2a and 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical structure elucidation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Three isolates (s3b09, s3b10, s3b12), all originating from the same soil sample, had an identical pyoverdine type (3).
source: Three isolates (s3b09, s3b10, s3b12), all originating from the same soil sample, had an identical pyoverdine type (3).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical structure elucidation data.

claim: Inhibitory pyoverdines had significantly larger collision-cross sections (CCS in Å2) than non-inhibitory ones (F1,22 = 10.63, p=.0036).
source: We found that inhibitory pyoverdines had significantly larger collision-cross sections (CCS in Å2) than non-inhibitory ones (F1,22 = 10.63, p=.0036, measured by ion mobility spectrometry [IMS]) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CCS values correlate with the volume of a molecule.
source: As CCS values correlate with the volume of a molecule, our results suggest that inhibitory pyoverdines are larger and have more complex molecule structures than non-inhibitory pyoverdines.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CCS measurements.

claim: Inhibitory pyoverdines are larger and have more complex molecule structures than non-inhibitory pyoverdines.
source: As CCS values correlate with the volume of a molecule, our results suggest that inhibitory pyoverdines are larger and have more complex molecule structures than non-inhibitory pyoverdines.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the CCS data.

claim: There was no significant difference between the two classes of pyoverdines regarding molecule polarity (F1,22 = 2.00, p=0.1711).
source: In contrast, there was no significant difference between the two classes of pyoverdines regarding molecule polarity (F1,22 = 2.00, p=0.1711, assessed by the chromatographic retention time [RT] on a reversed-phase column) (Figure 2C), but molecule polarity was significantly higher for ferri- than for apo-pyoverdines (F1,22 = 12.78, p=0.0017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Molecule polarity was significantly higher for ferri- than for apo-pyoverdines (F1,22 = 12.78, p=0.0017).
source: In contrast, there was no significant difference between the two classes of pyoverdines regarding molecule polarity (F1,22 = 2.00, p=0.1711, assessed by the chromatographic retention time [RT] on a reversed-phase column) (Figure 2C), but molecule polarity was significantly higher for ferri- than for apo-pyoverdines (F1,22 = 12.78, p=0.0017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Inhibitory pyoverdines are significantly more stable than non-inhibitory pyoverdines (F1,11 = 7.55, p=0.019) as measured by collision-induced unfolding.
source: We first measured the propensity of ferri-pyoverdines to undergo collision-induced unfolding (CIU) by IMS measurements at different Δ6 voltages and found that inhibitory pyoverdines are significantly more stable than non-inhibitory pyoverdines (F1,11 = 7.55, p=0.019) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The difference in CE50 between inhibitory and non-inhibitory pyoverdines was not significant (F1,11 = 1.87, p=0.198).
source: The same trend was observed for our second measure of stability (CE50, normalized collision energy (NCE) necessary to fragment 50% of ferri-pyoverdines), but in this case, the difference between the two pyoverdine classes was not significant (F1,11 = 1.87, p=0.198) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Inhibitory pyoverdines are larger and have a higher affinity for iron than non-inhibitory pyoverdines.
source: Taken together, the chemical analyses suggest that inhibitory pyoverdines are larger and have a higher affinity for iron than non-inhibitory pyoverdines.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the chemical analysis data.

claim: Ferribactin is the final pyoverdine precursor.
source: During HPLC purification, we observed that ferribactin (the final pyoverdine precursor) was also highly abundant in the supernatant (Budzikiewicz et al., 2007; Nadal-Jimenez et al., 2014), presumably released by cells during the centrifugation process.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Budzikiewicz et al., 2007 and Nadal-Jimenez et al., 2014.

claim: Ferribactin is typically not secreted but matures into pyoverdine in the periplasma.
source: This precursor is typically not secreted but matures into pyoverdine in the periplasma (Sugue et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sugue et al., 2022.

claim: Ferribactin has compromised iron-binding capacity.
source: Due to its compromised iron-binding capacity, we used it as a negative control for which no activity against pathogens is expected (Nadal-Jimenez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nadal-Jimenez et al., 2014.

claim: For A. baumannii and S. aureus, classical dose–response curves were observed in all pyoverdine assays, characterized by a decrease in bacterial growth at low and intermediate concentrations, followed by a complete halt of bacterial growth at higher pyoverdine concentrations.
source: For A. baumannii and S. aureus, we observed classical dose–response curves in all pyoverdine assays, characterized by a decrease in bacterial growth at low and intermediate concentrations, followed by a complete halt of bacterial growth at higher pyoverdine concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The IC50 value for pyoverdine s3b09 is 5.037 µg/mL for A. baumannii.
source: In contrast, the pyoverdine concentration is absolute for the HPLC-purified version, allowing the determination of an IC50 value for pyoverdine s3b09, which is 5.037 µg/mL and 12.163 µg/mL for A. baumannii and S. aureus, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dose-response curves.

claim: The IC50 value for pyoverdine s3b09 is 12.163 µg/mL for S. aureus.
source: In contrast, the pyoverdine concentration is absolute for the HPLC-purified version, allowing the determination of an IC50 value for pyoverdine s3b09, which is 5.037 µg/mL and 12.163 µg/mL for A. baumannii and S. aureus, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dose-response curves.

claim: For K. pneumoniae, the pyoverdines were less effective in reducing pathogen growth.
source: For K. pneumoniae, the pyoverdines were less effective in reducing pathogen growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: K. pneumoniae produces enterobactin, a siderophore that has higher iron affinity than pyoverdine.
source: One reason why pyoverdines might be less effective against K. pneumoniae is that this species produces enterobactin, a siderophore that has higher iron affinity than pyoverdine (Harris et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 1979.

claim: For P. aeruginosa, all pyoverdines were growth inhibitory at intermediate concentrations.
source: For P. aeruginosa, we observed that all pyoverdines were growth inhibitory at intermediate concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The initial inhibition converted into growth promotions at high pyoverdine concentrations in three out of four cases for P. aeruginosa.
source: The initial inhibition converted into growth promotions at high pyoverdine concentrations in three out of four cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: P. aeruginosa possesses two receptors (FpvA and FpvB) for pyoverdine uptake.
source: One reason for these non-standard dose–response curves could be that P. aeruginosa possesses two receptors (FpvA and FpvB) for pyoverdine uptake (Ghysels et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ghysels et al., 2004.

claim: P. aeruginosa may capitalize on the supplemented pyoverdines, especially at high concentrations via the upregulation of the heterologous promiscuous FpvB receptor.
source: It might thus capitalize on the supplemented pyoverdines, especially at high concentrations via the upregulation of the heterologous promiscuous FpvB receptor (González et al., 2021; Sexton et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to González et al., 2021 and Sexton et al., 2017.

claim: All pyoverdines are highly potent against A. baumannii and S. aureus.
source: Taken together, we found that all pyoverdines are highly potent against A. baumannii and S. aureus, and one pyoverdine (3G07) is potent against K. pneumoniae.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: One pyoverdine (3G07) is potent against K. pneumoniae.
source: Taken together, we found that all pyoverdines are highly potent against A. baumannii and S. aureus, and one pyoverdine (3G07) is potent against K. pneumoniae.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: No growth inhibition was found when the pathogens were exposed to purified ferribactin.
source: In support of our hypothesis that the inhibitory effects of pyoverdines operate via withholding iron from pathogens, we found no growth inhibition when the pathogens were exposed to purified ferribactin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the non-iron chelating precursor of pyoverdine.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inhibition of A. baumannii was greatly reduced with intermediate levels of iron supplementation (40 µm) and completely stalled with high levels of iron supplementation (200 µM).
source: Indeed, we observed that the inhibition of A. baumannii was greatly reduced with intermediate levels of iron supplementation (40 µm) and completely stalled with high levels of iron supplementation (200 µM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No adverse effects on cell viability were observed at low and intermediate pyoverdine concentrations for NSC-34 cells.
source: For these cells, we observed no adverse effects on cell viability at low and intermediate pyoverdine concentrations (Figure 4A), representing the doses that strongly inhibited the pathogens (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A moderate decrease in cell viability was only observed at the highest pyoverdine concentrations for NSC-34 cells.
source: A moderate decrease in cell viability was only observed at the highest pyoverdine concentrations (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A more pronounced effect on cell viability was noticed already at intermediate pyoverdine concentrations for HEK-293 cells.
source: Conversely, HEK-293 cells divide rapidly and inform us on whether pyoverdines interfere with cell proliferation. We indeed noticed a more pronounced effect on cell viability already at intermediate pyoverdine concentrations (Figure 4A), which suggests that pyoverdine chelates the iron required for cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pyoverdine chelates the iron required for cell proliferation in HEK-293 cells.
source: Conversely, HEK-293 cells divide rapidly and inform us on whether pyoverdines interfere with cell proliferation. We indeed noticed a more pronounced effect on cell viability already at intermediate pyoverdine concentrations (Figure 4A), which suggests that pyoverdine chelates the iron required for cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Hemolysis was extremely low (<1%) relative to the positive control Triton X-100 surfactant for pyoverdine concentrations up to 0.5.
source: We found that hemolysis was extremely low (<1%) relative to the positive control Triton X-100 surfactant for pyoverdine concentrations up to 0.5 (Figure 4B) and remained low even for the highest concentration (hemolysis rates for pyoverdines 3A06, 3G07, and s3b09 were 2.01, 1.89, and 5.92%, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Pyoverdines are unable to retrieve iron from hemoglobin.
source: This result shows that pyoverdines are unable to retrieve iron from hemoglobin.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the hemolysis assay results.

claim: Pyoverdine injections did not significantly reduce host survival at low and intermediate concentrations.
source: We found that pyoverdine injections did not significantly reduce host survival at low and intermediate concentrations (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A tendency toward higher larval mortality levels was observed with the highest pyoverdine concentration administered, especially for 3G07.
source: In contrast, we observed a tendency toward higher larval mortality levels with the highest pyoverdine concentration administered, especially for 3G07, suggesting that pyoverdines can be mildly toxic for the host at high concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Pyoverdines can be mildly toxic for the host at high concentrations.
source: In contrast, we observed a tendency toward higher larval mortality levels with the highest pyoverdine concentration administered, especially for 3G07, suggesting that pyoverdines can be mildly toxic for the host at high concentrations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The two pyoverdines 3A06 and 3G07 were effective treatments against A. baumannii and K. pneumoniae and significantly decreased the risk of death compared to untreated infections.
source: We found that the two pyoverdines 3A06 and 3G07 were effective treatments against A. baumannii and K. pneumoniae and significantly decreased the risk of death compared to untreated infections (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A. baumannii treated with 3A06 at a concentration of 0.05 reduced the risk of death (hazard) by 57.9% (z = –1.973, p=0.0485).
source: Specifically, A. baumannii treated with 3A06 at a concentration of 0.05 and 3G07 at a concentration of 0.01 reduced the risk of death (hazard) by 57.9% (z = –1.973, p=0.0485) and 59.4% (z = –2.057, p=0.0397), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Cox proportional hazard regressions.

claim: A. baumannii treated with 3G07 at a concentration of 0.01 reduced the risk of death (hazard) by 59.4% (z = –2.057, p=0.0397).
source: Specifically, A. baumannii treated with 3A06 at a concentration of 0.05 and 3G07 at a concentration of 0.01 reduced the risk of death (hazard) by 57.9% (z = –1.973, p=0.0485) and 59.4% (z = –2.057, p=0.0397), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Cox proportional hazard regressions.

claim: For K. pneumoniae, the pyoverdine treatments 3A06 and 3G07 (concentration of 0.01) reduced the risk of death by 51.5% (z = –2.027, p=0.0426) and 57.6% (z = –2.341, p=0.0192), respectively.
source: For K. pneumoniae, the pyoverdine treatments 3A06 and 3G07 (concentration of 0.01) reduced the risk of death by 51.5% (z = –2.027, p=0.0426) and 57.6% (z = –2.341, p=0.0192), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Cox proportional hazard regressions.

claim: Low and intermediate doses of pyoverdine are more effective than the highest concentration.
source: These results suggest that low and intermediate doses of pyoverdine are more effective than the highest concentration.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Hump-shaped relationships were found between pyoverdine concentrations and time-to-death in four out of six cases with two of them being significant.
source: We found hump-shaped relationships between pyoverdine concentrations and time-to-death in four out of six cases with two of them being significant (quadratic regression models for K. pneumoniae treated with pyoverdine 3G07: linear term: F1,71 = 0.88, p=0.3506, quadratic term: F1,71 = 6.11, p=0.0159 and s3b09: linear term: F1,73 = 0.31, p=0.5806, quadratic term: F1,73 = 6.16, p=0.0153).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Infections with P. aeruginosa led to near 100% larval mortality regardless of pyoverdine treatment and dosage.
source: In contrast, infections with P. aeruginosa led to near 100% larval mortality regardless of pyoverdine treatment and dosage so that no significant treatment effect arose (Figure 5) and no effect on the time-to-death of larvae could be observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Pyoverdines are effective against the moderately virulent pathogens A. baumannii and K. pneumoniae by decreasing the risk of death by more than 50%.
source: Altogether, our infection experiments show that pyoverdines are effective against the moderately virulent pathogens A. baumannii and K. pneumoniae by decreasing the risk of death by more than 50%, while they are ineffective against the fast-killing highly virulent P. aeruginosa.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Pyoverdines are ineffective against the fast-killing highly virulent P. aeruginosa.
source: Altogether, our infection experiments show that pyoverdines are effective against the moderately virulent pathogens A. baumannii and K. pneumoniae by decreasing the risk of death by more than 50%, while they are ineffective against the fast-killing highly virulent P. aeruginosa.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Intermediate pyoverdine concentrations are most effective.
source: Moreover, intermediate pyoverdine concentration are most effective, reinforcing our observation that pyoverdine can exhibit some toxicity at higher concentrations (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: All four pathogens grew significantly better under ciprofloxacin treatment than the ancestor and beyond the level observed for growth medium adaptation.
source: After experimental evolution, we observed that all four pathogens grew significantly better under ciprofloxacin treatment than the ancestor and beyond the level observed for growth medium adaptation (Supplementary file 1c; Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is strong evidence for pervasive resistance evolution against ciprofloxacin.
source: This provides strong evidence for pervasive resistance evolution against this conventional antibiotic.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental evolution data.

claim: None of the four pathogens treated with pyoverdines experienced a significant increase in growth relative to the observed level of growth medium adaptation.
